examples.en: The kids keep chattering away in the classroom.

examples.ko: 동생은 학교에서 있었던 일을 저한테 다 조잘거려요.
examples.en: My younger sibling babbles to me about everything that happened at school.
The birds have been twittering outside the window since morning.
What are you two chattering about like that?

examples.ko: 딸이 차 안에서 내내 조잘거려서 안 심심했어요.
examples.en: My daughter chattered the whole time in the car, so I wasn't bored.

examples.ko: 수업 시간에는 조잘거리지 말고 조용히 해요.
examples.en: Don't chatter during class; be quiet.

explain: 주로 아이나 새처럼 작고 귀여운 대상이 쉬지 않고 말하거나 지저귈 때 써요. 큰 소리로 시끄럽게 떠드는 느낌이면 '떠들다'가 더 잘 맞아요. '재잘거리다'도 비슷하게 쓰고 '조잘대다'와는 바꿔 쓸 수 있어요.
explain_en: It is mostly used when children or birds keep talking or chirping in a small, lively way. If the noise is loud and annoying, '떠들다' fits better. '재잘거리다' is used in a similar way, and it can be swapped with '조잘대다'.

examples.en: The kindergarten kids chatter next to their teacher.

examples.ko: 친구들이 점심시간 내내 조잘대서 정신이 없었어요.
examples.en: My friends chattered all through lunch, so it was hectic.

examples.ko: 조카는 만나기만 하면 쉬지 않고 조잘대요.
examples.en: My nephew babbles non-stop whenever we meet.
I can hear sparrows twittering on the branches.
Someone in the back seat keeps chattering.
My younger sibling was chattering excitedly and ended up falling asleep.

explain: '조잘거리다'와 뜻이 거의 같아서 바꿔 써도 돼요. 아이나 새가 끊임없이 재미있게 이야기하거나 지저귀는 모습에 잘 어울려요. 어른에게 쓰면 수다스럽다는 느낌이 있어서 말투에 조심해요.
explain_en: It means almost the same as '조잘거리다' and the two can be swapped. It suits children or birds who keep chatting or chirping cheerfully. Used for adults, it can sound like they are too talkative, so be careful with your tone.

examples.en: The union and the company finally agreed on the compromise proposal.
The government announced a new compromise proposal yesterday.

examples.ko: 이 조정안은 양쪽 모두에게 불리하지 않아요.
examples.en: This compromise proposal isn't unfavorable to either side.
We are reviewing the compromise proposal the committee put forward.
As soon as the proposal came out, there was a lot of opposition.

examples.ko: 우리 팀은 일정 조정안을 따로 준비했어요.
examples.en: Our team prepared a separate proposal to adjust the schedule.

explain: 서로 다른 의견이나 이해관계를 맞추려고 내놓는 계획이나 제안에 써요. '조정안을 내놓다·제시하다·받아들이다'처럼 뉴스에서 자주 들어요. '타협안', '중재안'도 비슷하게 쓰지만 '조정안'은 일정·예산·규정 등을 고치는 경우에도 써요.
explain_en: It is used for a plan or proposal made to bring different opinions or interests together. You often hear it in the news in phrases like '조정안을 내놓다', '제시하다' and '받아들이다'. '타협안' and '중재안' are similar, but '조정안' can also be used when adjusting schedules, budgets or rules.

examples.ko: 우리 팀은 개인 실력보다 조직력이 더 강해요.
examples.en: Our team is stronger in organizational cohesion than in individual skill.
The secret to winning the game was the players' teamwork and organization.
As the company grew, its organizational strength weakened.

examples.ko: 조직력을 키우려면 먼저 서로 믿어야 해요.
examples.en: To build organizational strength, you first have to trust each other.

examples.ko: 이 동아리는 조직력이 좋아서 행사를 잘 해요.
examples.en: This club is well organized, so it runs events well.

examples.ko: 수비 조직력이 흔들려서 두 골이나 내줬어요.
examples.en: Our defensive organization fell apart and we gave up two goals.

explain: 팀이나 단체가 여러 사람을 짜임새 있게 움직이게 하는 힘을 말할 때 써요. 스포츠 뉴스에서 '수비 조직력'처럼 자주 나오고, 개인 능력을 말하는 '개인기'와 대비해서 쓰기도 해요. '조직력이 좋다·강하다·흔들리다'와 같이 써요.
explain_en: It is used for a team's or group's ability to make many people move in a well-structured way. It often appears in sports news, as in '수비 조직력', and is sometimes contrasted with '개인기' (individual skill). It goes with '좋다', '강하다' and '흔들리다'.

examples.en: The organizing of citizens is moving along quickly.

examples.ko: 자료의 조직화가 잘 안 돼서 발표가 헷갈렸어요.
examples.en: The material wasn't well organized, so the presentation was confusing.
Organizing workers is not easy.
Volunteer activities need to be organized.

examples.ko: 조직화가 잘된 팀은 일을 빨리 끝내요.
examples.en: A well-organized team finishes work quickly.
I learned how to organize information in class.

explain: 사람이나 생각, 자료를 체계 있게 짜는 일을 말해요. 주로 글이나 뉴스, 수업에서 쓰고, 일상 대화에서는 '정리하다', '모으다'처럼 풀어서 말할 때가 많아요. '조직화가 필요하다·잘되다'와 같이 써요.
explain_en: It refers to arranging people, ideas or materials in a systematic way. It is mostly used in writing, news and classes, and in everyday talk people often say things like '정리하다' or '모으다' instead. It goes with '필요하다' and '잘되다'.

examples.en: The students organize the group by themselves.
Try organizing the material by topic.

examples.ko: 주민들이 힘을 모아 반대 운동을 조직화했어요.
examples.en: The residents joined forces and organized the protest movement.
You need practice organizing your thoughts.

examples.ko: 팀장이 업무를 조직화하지 못해서 늘 바빠요.
examples.en: The team leader can't organize the work, so everyone is always busy.
If you organize your schedule in advance, you save time.

explain: 흩어진 사람이나 생각, 자료를 체계 있게 묶는다는 느낌이에요. 글이나 설명에서 많이 쓰고, 일상 대화에서는 '정리하다', '짜다'라고 더 자주 말해요. '모임을 조직하다'는 새로 만든다는 느낌이고, '조직화하다'는 이미 있는 것을 체계 있게 만든다는 느낌이 강해요.
explain_en: It gives the feeling of bringing scattered people, ideas or materials together in a systematic way. It is common in writing and explanations, while in everyday talk people more often say '정리하다' or '짜다'. '모임을 조직하다' feels like setting up something new, while '조직화하다' leans toward giving structure to what already exists.

examples.ko: 내일 아침 일곱 시에 조찬 모임이 있어요.
examples.en: I have a breakfast meeting at seven tomorrow morning.
The president is holding a breakfast meeting at a hotel.
I got up early to attend the breakfast lecture.
The politicians gathered and had breakfast together.

examples.ko: 이번 조찬 간담회에서는 경제 이야기가 나왔어요.
examples.en: The economy came up at this breakfast talk.
Breakfast at these meetings is usually a light meal.

explain: 혼자 먹는 평범한 아침 식사에는 쓰지 않고, 아침에 모여서 하는 모임이나 행사에 붙여서 써요. '조찬 모임·조찬 회의·조찬 강연'처럼 뉴스나 회사에서 자주 들어요. 일상에서 아침을 먹는다고 할 때는 '아침 식사'나 '아침'이라고 해요.
explain_en: It is not used for an ordinary breakfast you eat alone, but for morning gatherings or events. You often hear it in news and at work, as in '조찬 모임', '조찬 회의' and '조찬 강연'. For eating breakfast in daily life, people say '아침 식사' or '아침'.

examples.en: Grandma gave me rice cake sticks to dip in jocheong.

examples.ko: 이 한과에는 조청이 듬뿍 들어 있어요.
examples.en: This traditional sweet has plenty of jocheong in it.
I used jocheong instead of taffy to add sweetness.
Jocheong is made from rice or barley.
I bought a bottle of jocheong at the market.

examples.ko: 떡볶이에 설탕 대신 조청을 넣어 봤어요.
examples.en: I tried putting jocheong in the tteokbokki instead of sugar.

explain: '엿'과 비슷하지만 더 묽어서 떡을 찍어 먹거나 요리에 넣을 때 써요. 전통 음식이나 한과 이야기에 나와요.
explain_en: It is similar to '엿' (Korean taffy) but runnier, so people dip rice cakes in it or use it in cooking. It comes up when talking about traditional food and 한과.

examples.en: We play jokgu on the field every lunch break.
Our department won the jokgu tournament.

examples.ko: 족구는 손을 못 쓰는데 생각보다 힘들어요.
examples.en: In jokgu you can't use your hands, and it's harder than it looks.

examples.ko: 군대에서 족구를 자주 했다고 아빠가 말했어요.
examples.en: Dad said he often played jokgu in the army.

examples.ko: 이번 주말에 족구 한 판 할래요?
examples.en: Do you want to play a game of jokgu this weekend?
I hurt my ankle playing jokgu at lunchtime.

explain: 발과 머리로 공을 네트 위로 넘기는 한국식 구기 운동이에요. 학교, 군대, 회사에서 점심시간에 많이 하는 운동으로 알려져 있어요. '족구를 하다'라고 말하고, '차다'만 쓰면 어색해요.
explain_en: It is a Korean ball sport where players send the ball over a net using their feet and head. It is known as something people play at school, in the military and at work during lunch. You say '족구를 하다'; using only '차다' sounds odd.

examples.ko: 혼례를 올리는 날 신랑은 사모관대를, 신부는 족두리를 쓰고 원삼을 입었어요.
examples.en: On the wedding day, the groom wore a samo gwandae, and the bride wore a jokduri and a wonsam.

examples.ko: 박물관에서 보석이 달린 예쁜 족두리를 구경했어요.
examples.en: I looked at a pretty jokduri decorated with jewels at the museum.

examples.ko: 신부가 머리에 족두리를 쓰고 앉아 있어요.
examples.en: The bride is sitting with a jokduri on her head.
Some jokduri are decorated with jewels.
I also rented a jokduri at the hanbok rental shop.
I heard the jokduri was so heavy that it was hard to bow her head.

explain: 전통 혼례에서 신부가 머리에 쓰는 장식 모자예요. 옷은 '입다', 족두리는 머리에 얹으니 '쓰다'를 써요. 요즘은 전통 혼례 체험이나 사극, 박물관에서 만날 수 있어요.
explain_en: It is a decorative headpiece a bride wears in a traditional wedding. Clothes take '입다', but a jokduri sits on the head, so you use '쓰다'. Today you can see it at traditional wedding experiences, in historical dramas and in museums.

examples.ko: 여기서 역까지 족히 삼십 분은 걸려요.
examples.en: It takes a good thirty minutes at least from here to the station.

examples.ko: 그 나무는 높이가 족히 십 미터는 돼요.
examples.en: That tree is easily ten meters tall.
At least a hundred guests came.

examples.ko: 이 책을 다 읽으려면 족히 일주일은 필요해요.
examples.en: You'll need a good week at least to finish this book.

examples.ko: 그 사람 나이가 족히 쉰은 넘어 보여요.
examples.en: He looks easily over fifty.
The luggage must be at least twenty boxes.

explain: '적어도'와 비슷하지만 '그 정도는 넉넉히 된다'는 느낌이 있어서 놀라거나 많다고 느낄 때 어울려요. 뒤에 숫자나 수량 표현이 오고 '-은/는'이 자주 붙어요. '족히 한 시간은 걸려요'처럼 말해요.
explain_en: It is similar to '적어도' (at least), but it carries the feeling of 'easily that much', so it fits when you are surprised or feel it is a lot. A number or quantity comes after it, and '-은/는' is often attached. For example, '족히 한 시간은 걸려요'.

examples.en: Whether to keep or abolish this department is being discussed.
It is an important meeting that will decide whether the company survives.
Citizens gathered over the issue of whether to keep the library.
Many shops are at risk of shutting down.

examples.ko: 그 제도의 존폐를 두고 의견이 갈려요.
examples.en: Opinions are split over whether to keep or scrap that system.

examples.ko: 학교 존폐 여부는 다음 달에 정해져요.
examples.en: Whether the school stays open will be decided next month.

explain: 어떤 기관이나 제도를 계속 둘지 없앨지가 걸린 상황에 써요. '존폐 위기', '존폐 논란'처럼 뉴스에서 자주 나오고, 보통 '존폐가', '존폐를'처럼 다른 말과 함께 써요.
explain_en: It is used when it is at stake whether an institution or system will continue or be abolished. It often appears in the news in phrases like '존폐 위기' and '존폐 논란', and it is usually used together with other words, as in '존폐가' and '존폐를'.

examples.ko: 더운 날 행사장에서 졸도 환자가 여러 명 나왔어요.
examples.en: Several people fainted at the event on the hot day.

examples.ko: 할아버지가 졸도로 쓰러지셔서 병원에 실려 가셨어요.
examples.en: Grandpa collapsed in a faint and was taken to the hospital.

examples.ko: 졸도 소식을 듣고 가족들이 급히 달려왔어요.
examples.en: Hearing the news of the faint, the family rushed over.

examples.ko: 선생님은 졸도 증상이 있으면 바로 눕히라고 했어요.
examples.en: The teacher said to lay the person down right away if there are signs of fainting.
Everyone was shocked by the sudden faint.

examples.ko: 졸도를 막으려면 물을 자주 마셔야 해요.
examples.en: To avoid fainting, you should drink water often.

explain: '기절'과 비슷하지만 '졸도'는 뉴스나 글에서 더 자주 보여요. 일상 대화에서는 '기절하다', '쓰러지다'라고 말할 때가 많아요. 동사로는 '졸도하다'를 써요.
explain_en: It is similar to '기절' but appears more in news and writing. In daily conversation people more often say '기절하다' or '쓰러지다'. The verb form is '졸도하다'.

examples.en: I was so shocked that I almost fainted.
A student fainted in the heat.
She suddenly fainted, so an ambulance came.
If you fast too hard, you might faint.
I got a call saying my father had fainted.
Get enough sleep so you don't faint.

explain: 일상에서는 '기절하다'나 '쓰러지다'를 더 많이 써요. '졸도할 뻔했다'는 너무 놀랐다는 과장된 말로도 자주 써요. 윗사람에게는 '졸도하시다'로 높여요.
explain_en: In daily life people more often use '기절하다' or '쓰러지다'. '졸도할 뻔했다' is also often used as an exaggeration for being extremely shocked. For someone older or senior, it becomes '졸도하시다'.

examples.ko: 허리띠를 졸라매고 한 달만 아껴 봐요.
examples.en: Tighten your belt and try saving for just a month.
I tied my shoelaces tightly.
Please cinch the mouth of the sack shut with a string.
My pay has gone down, so I have to tighten my belt.
The backpack shakes less when I tighten the straps.
The child pulled the drawstring of his pants tight and ran out.

explain: 끈이나 줄을 힘주어 당겨 단단히 묶을 때 써요. '묶다'보다 꽉 조이는 느낌이 강해요. '허리띠를 졸라매다'는 돈을 아낀다는 뜻으로 많이 말해요.

phrases.example: 요즘 물가가 올라서 다들 허리띠를 졸라매고 있어요.
phrases.en: With prices rising these days, everyone is tightening their belts.
phrases.nuance_ko: 실제로 허리띠를 조이는 게 아니라, 돈을 아끼고 어려운 시기를 참고 견딘다는 뜻으로 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: It does not mean literally tightening a belt; it means cutting back on spending and enduring a hard period.

explain_en: It is used when you pull a string or strap hard and tie it firmly. It feels tighter than '묶다'. '허리띠를 졸라매다' is very often used to mean saving money.

examples.en: Breaking a promise and then making excuses is petty.

examples.ko: 남의 잘못만 캐는 건 졸렬한 행동이에요.
examples.en: Digging only for other people's faults is mean behavior.
Don't hide in a cowardly way; apologize in person.

examples.ko: 그런 졸렬한 방법으로 이기고 싶지 않아요.
examples.en: I don't want to win by such a low method.
Everyone was disappointed by his pettiness.

examples.ko: 일을 떠넘기는 태도가 너무 졸렬하게 느껴졌어요.
examples.en: Passing the work off onto others felt really petty.

explain: 사람의 마음이나 행동, 방법이 비겁하고 쩨쩨할 때 써요. 말투가 꽤 강해서 사람 앞에서 직접 쓰면 심한 비난으로 들려요. 가볍게 말할 때는 '치사하다'를 더 많이 써요.
explain_en: It is used when a person's attitude, actions or methods are cowardly and petty. The tone is quite strong, so saying it directly to someone sounds like a harsh accusation. In casual talk people use '치사하다' more.

examples.en: In the army, I was the lowest-ranking soldier.

examples.ko: 졸병 시절에는 선임들 눈치를 많이 봤대요.
examples.en: I heard he was always watching his seniors' moods in his low-rank days.

examples.ko: 졸병이 장군에게 직접 말을 걸 수는 없어요.
examples.en: A low-ranking soldier can't speak directly to a general.
My father started his military life as a low-ranking soldier.
The privates stood guard all night.

examples.ko: 졸병 때 먹은 라면 맛을 못 잊겠어요.
examples.en: I can't forget the taste of the ramyeon I ate as a private.

explain: 계급이 낮은 병사를 말하고, 반대는 '고참'이에요. 입말로는 '쫄병'이라고도 해요. 군대 밖에서도 회사나 모임에서 가장 아랫사람을 농담처럼 가리킬 때 쓰기도 해요.
explain_en: It refers to a soldier of low rank, and its opposite is '고참' (veteran). In speech it is also said '쫄병'. Outside the military, it is sometimes used jokingly for the lowest-ranking person at work or in a group.

examples.ko: 갑자기 돈을 번 졸부라고 소문이 났어요.
examples.en: Rumor spread that he is a nouveau riche who suddenly made money.
He shows off expensive cars like a nouveau riche.
The outfit looked like someone who had newly become rich.

examples.ko: 복권에 당첨되어 졸부가 된 사람이 있어요.
examples.en: There's someone who won the lottery and became suddenly rich.
I heard he felt bad about being treated like a nouveau riche.

examples.ko: 드라마에는 졸부 집안 이야기가 자주 나와요.
examples.en: Stories about newly rich families often appear in dramas.

explain: 갑자기 부자가 된 사람을 조금 깎아내리는 느낌으로 말해요. '벼락부자'와 비슷하지만 '졸부'는 품위나 취향이 없다는 비웃음이 더 들어 있어요. 사람 앞에서 직접 쓰면 무례해요.
explain_en: It describes someone who suddenly became rich, with a slightly belittling tone. It is similar to '벼락부자', but '졸부' carries more of a sneer that the person lacks refinement or taste. Saying it to someone's face is rude.

examples.en: After boiling the stew a long time, the broth cooked down.
When the water boils down, please turn the heat down.
Boil the soup until it reduces by half.
The reservoir water is drying down in the drought.
The sauce reduced and the color got darker.

examples.ko: 냄비 속 물이 거의 졸아들어서 깜짝 놀랐어요.
examples.en: The water in the pot had almost boiled away, which startled me.

explain: 끓이거나 말라서 물이나 국물이 줄어들 때 써요. 그냥 양이 줄 때 쓰는 '줄다'와 달리 끓거나 마르는 상황에 어울려요. 사람이 일부러 졸일 때는 타동사 '졸이다'를 써서 '찌개를 졸이다'라고 해요.
explain_en: It is used when liquid or broth gets smaller through boiling or drying. Unlike '줄다', which is for any decrease in amount, it fits boiling or drying situations. When a person does it on purpose, the transitive verb '졸이다' is used, as in '찌개를 졸이다'.

examples.en: The old sweater in the closet got moth-eaten.

examples.ko: 오래된 책이 좀먹어서 글자가 안 보여요.
examples.en: The old book is eaten by pests, so I can't see the letters.
The wooden box was being eaten away from the inside.
I think false rumors eat away at society.
Suspicion slowly eats away at our relationship.
It's better to throw away a moth-eaten blanket.

explain: 좀(옷이나 책을 갉아 먹는 작은 벌레)이 먹어서 상하는 것을 말해요. 그래서 '옷이 좀먹다', '책이 좀먹다'처럼 쓰고, 눈에 잘 안 띄게 조금씩 망가질 때 비유로도 써요. 비유로 쓸 때는 보통 '~을 좀먹다'처럼 목적어를 붙여요.

phrases.en: False information eats away at society.
phrases.nuance_ko: 벌레가 먹는 것처럼 눈에 띄지 않게 천천히 안에서부터 해를 입힌다는 뜻이에요. 주로 부정적인 것이 대상을 망가뜨릴 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: It means slowly harming something from the inside without being noticed, like insects at work. It is mainly used when a negative thing damages its target.

explain_en: It describes things being damaged by '좀', small insects that gnaw clothes and books. So you say '옷이 좀먹다' or '책이 좀먹다', and it is also used figuratively when something is slowly ruined without being noticed. In the figurative use, it usually takes an object, as in '~을 좀먹다'.

examples.en: I put a mothball in the closet.

examples.ko: 좀약 냄새가 너무 강해서 창문을 열었어요.
examples.en: The mothball smell was so strong that I opened the window.
I put away the winter clothes and added a mothball too.

examples.ko: 할머니 집 서랍에서 좀약 냄새가 났어요.
examples.en: The drawer at Grandma's house smelled of mothballs.

examples.ko: 좀약은 아이 손이 닿지 않는 곳에 두세요.
examples.en: Keep mothballs out of children's reach.

examples.ko: 좀약이 다 떨어져서 새로 사 왔어요.
examples.en: We ran out of mothballs, so I bought new ones.

explain: 옷장에 넣어 옷을 벌레에게서 지키는 약이에요. 요즘 가게에서는 '방충제'라는 이름으로 파는 경우가 많아요. 냄새가 강해서 '좀약 냄새'라는 말을 자주 해요.
explain_en: It is a product put in a closet to protect clothes from insects. Today stores often sell it under the name '방충제'. Because the smell is strong, people often say '좀약 냄새'.
